apis.name: CreateThread
apis.summary: Creates a thread that begins execution in the calling process.
apis.description: CreateThread creates a new thread in the calling process and starts it at an application-defined start routine, unless CREATE_SUSPENDED is specified. The new thread shares the process address space, handles, and other resources with the existing threads. The caller receives a handle to the thread and, optionally, the system-wide thread identifier. The thread runs until its start routine returns, it calls ExitThread, or the process terminates.
apis.prototype: HANDLE CreateThread(LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpThreadAttributes, SIZE_T dwStackSize, LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE lpStartAddress, LPVOID lpParameter, DWORD dwCreationFlags, LPDWORD lpThreadId);

parameters.name: lpThreadAttributes
parameters.description: Optional SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES for the new thread object. NULL gives the thread a default security descriptor and a non-inheritable handle.

parameters.name: dwStackSize
parameters.description: The initial stack size, in bytes. The system rounds the value to the nearest page. Zero selects the default size for the executable. Unless STACK_SIZE_PARAM_IS_A_RESERVATION is set in dwCreationFlags, the value is treated as the initial committed stack size.

parameters.name: lpStartAddress
parameters.description: A pointer to the application-defined function that the thread executes. The function receives lpParameter and returns a DWORD exit code.

parameters.name: lpParameter
parameters.description: A single pointer-sized value passed to the thread function. It may be NULL. The value and any memory it points to must remain valid for as long as the thread uses them.

parameters.name: dwCreationFlags
parameters.description: Flags that control thread creation. Zero starts the thread immediately; CREATE_SUSPENDED creates the thread suspended until ResumeThread is called. STACK_SIZE_PARAM_IS_A_RESERVATION changes how dwStackSize is interpreted.

parameters.name: lpThreadId
parameters.description: Optional pointer that receives the new thread's identifier. It may be NULL when the identifier is not needed. The identifier is valid only while the thread exists.

return.success: A handle to the new thread. Close it with CloseHandle when it is no longer needed.
return.failure: NULL. Call GetLastError for the error code.

apis.remarks: Code that calls C/C++ runtime library functions from the new thread should normally use _beginthreadex so the runtime can initialize and tear down per-thread state. CreateThread remains appropriate for code that does not depend on that per-thread state. Returning from the thread function and calling ExitThread both end the thread, but returning lets C++ destructors run.
apis.maldev_notes: CreateThread is ordinary in multithreaded software and also appears in analysis of code that starts work inside its own process. Analysts often note the start address, whether it lies in a loaded module or in dynamically allocated memory, the creation flags, and what the thread does next. The call alone does not indicate malicious behavior.
apis.defensive_notes: Thread-creation telemetry can record the creating process, the start address, and the new thread identifier. Comparing the start address with known module mappings and with expected software behavior is more informative than the presence of the call.

example.notes: The example creates one worker thread in the current process, waits up to five seconds for it to finish, and closes the thread handle. No special privileges are required. It is illustrative and is never executed by NtExplorer.

apis.name: OpenThread
apis.summary: Opens an existing thread by its identifier and returns a handle with the requested access rights.
apis.description: OpenThread obtains a handle to a thread from its system-wide thread identifier. The requested access rights determine which operations the caller can perform, such as querying information, suspending or resuming the thread, or reading and writing its context. The system checks the caller's token against the thread object's security descriptor, so some rights may be denied even when the identifier is valid.
apis.prototype: HANDLE OpenThread(DWORD dwDesiredAccess, BOOL bInheritHandle, DWORD dwThreadId);

parameters.name: dwDesiredAccess
parameters.description: The access rights to request. Common values include THREAD_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, THREAD_QUERY_INFORMATION, THREAD_SUSPEND_RESUME, THREAD_GET_CONTEXT, THREAD_SET_CONTEXT, and THREAD_TERMINATE. Request only the rights the task requires.

parameters.name: bInheritHandle
parameters.description: If TRUE, child processes can inherit the returned handle. Inheritance also requires that the handle be marked inheritable.

parameters.name: dwThreadId
parameters.description: The system-wide identifier of the thread to open. Thread identifiers can be reused after a thread terminates, so a stale value may refer to a different thread.

return.success: A handle to the thread with the granted access rights. Close it with CloseHandle when finished.

apis.remarks: A thread identifier is not a stable identity because it can be reused. When identity matters, verify properties such as the owning process and thread creation time in addition to the identifier. An open handle keeps the thread object alive after the thread itself has exited.
apis.maldev_notes: Opening a thread is a prerequisite for operations such as inspecting its context or changing its suspend count. Analysis usually considers the requested access mask, the target process, and whether the caller had a plausible reason to operate on that thread. The open call alone is not a behavioral verdict.
apis.defensive_notes: Thread-handle telemetry can expose cross-process access and unusual access masks. Correlating the requesting process, the target process, the granted rights, and subsequent operations is more useful than flagging the open call by itself.

example.title: Open the calling thread for a limited query
example.notes: The example opens the calling thread with the least-privilege query right, prints the identifier associated with the handle, and closes it. It is illustrative and is never executed by NtExplorer.

apis.source_notes: Access-right handling and identifier semantics checked against Microsoft Learn (processthreadsapi.h).

apis.name: GetCurrentThread
apis.summary: Returns a pseudo-handle that refers to the calling thread.
apis.description: GetCurrentThread returns a special constant that always refers to the thread making the call. It is not a real kernel handle and does not need to be closed. Functions that accept thread handles can use the pseudo-handle when they should operate on the caller rather than on another thread.

return.success: A pseudo-handle for the current thread, currently the constant (HANDLE)-2.

apis.remarks: Do not pass the pseudo-handle to CloseHandle. The value is meaningful only in the calling process and cannot be inherited. To obtain a real handle that can be used outside the calling thread, duplicate the pseudo-handle with DuplicateHandle.
apis.maldev_notes: Code that operates on its own thread often uses this call. It is a convenience for self-reference, not a behavioral signal in itself.
apis.defensive_notes: When reviewing thread operations, the current-thread pseudo-handle can help distinguish self-operations from operations on another thread.
apis.source_notes: Pseudo-handle value and lifetime rules checked against Microsoft Learn.

apis.name: GetCurrentThreadId
apis.summary: Returns the system-wide identifier of the calling thread.
apis.description: GetCurrentThreadId returns the identifier assigned to the calling thread. The identifier is unique across the system while the thread exists, but the system can reuse it after the thread terminates. It is commonly used for logging, naming synchronization objects, and locating the thread with OpenThread.

return.success: The thread identifier of the calling thread.

apis.remarks: A thread identifier is not a handle and cannot be used for operations that require one. Identifiers are reused after threads exit, so historical records should be correlated with process and timing information.
apis.maldev_notes: Thread identifiers are used for logging, object naming, and finding a thread to open. Their presence is ordinary; the relevant question is what the program does with the identifier.
apis.defensive_notes: Thread identifiers appear in many event records. Because they are reused, correlate them with the owning process, image path, and start time rather than treating them as globally stable.
apis.source_notes: Return type and identifier-reuse caveat checked against Microsoft Learn.

apis.name: GetThreadId
apis.summary: Returns the system-wide identifier associated with a thread handle.
apis.description: GetThreadId maps an open thread handle to the identifier assigned by the system. The handle must have THREAD_QUERY_INFORMATION or THREAD_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION access. The identifier remains valid only while the thread exists and can be reused afterwards.

parameters.name: Thread
parameters.description: A handle to the thread. It must have THREAD_QUERY_INFORMATION or THREAD_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION access.

apis.remarks: Check the return value against zero rather than assuming every failure is distinguishable from a valid identifier. This function is the thread counterpart of GetProcessId.
apis.maldev_notes: Converting a thread handle to an identifier is common when logging relationships between threads. On its own it does not indicate malicious behavior.
apis.defensive_notes: Correlating handles and identifiers can clarify which thread an event refers to, especially when handles were duplicated or inherited.

apis.name: SuspendThread
apis.summary: Increments a thread's suspend count, preventing it from being scheduled while the count is nonzero.
apis.description: SuspendThread increments the suspend count of the specified thread. A thread whose suspend count is greater than zero is not scheduled to run. The function returns the previous suspend count, which lets the caller detect nested suspensions. Each successful call must eventually be balanced by ResumeThread.

parameters.name: hThread
parameters.description: A handle to the thread to suspend. The handle must have THREAD_SUSPEND_RESUME access.

return.success: The thread's previous suspend count. A value greater than one means the thread was already suspended.

apis.remarks: SuspendThread is intended primarily for debuggers and is not a synchronization primitive. Suspending a thread that holds a lock or is executing inside a critical section can deadlock the process. A thread suspended at an arbitrary point may hold inconsistent application state until it is resumed.
apis.maldev_notes: SuspendThread appears in debuggers, process-control tools, and analysis of code that pauses another thread. Investigators usually examine which thread was suspended, the caller's access, and the surrounding sequence, because the call alone is ambiguous.
apis.defensive_notes: Thread-suspension activity can be observed through handle operations and thread state changes. Cross-process suspension of security or monitoring threads deserves context, but suspension also has routine debugging and instrumentation uses.
apis.source_notes: Suspend-count semantics and the debugger-oriented guidance checked against Microsoft Learn.

apis.name: ResumeThread
apis.summary: Decrements a thread's suspend count and allows the thread to run when the count reaches zero.
apis.description: ResumeThread decrements the suspend count of the specified thread. If the count reaches zero, the thread becomes eligible to be scheduled. The function returns the previous suspend count, so a caller can tell whether the thread was suspended once, several times, or not at all. Resuming a thread that is not suspended has no effect on its execution.

parameters.name: hThread
parameters.description: A handle to the thread to resume. The handle must have THREAD_SUSPEND_RESUME access.

return.success: The thread's previous suspend count. Zero means the thread was not suspended; one means it was suspended and is now eligible to run; a value greater than one means it remains suspended.

apis.remarks: ResumeThread does not guarantee that the thread runs immediately; it only makes the thread eligible for scheduling. Processes created with CREATE_SUSPENDED have a primary thread that must be resumed with this function before it executes.
apis.maldev_notes: ResumeThread is commonly paired with CREATE_SUSPENDED process creation and with debugger or instrumentation workflows. Analysis usually focuses on which thread is resumed and what the thread does immediately afterwards, not on the call in isolation.
apis.defensive_notes: Resuming a thread, especially the primary thread of a process created suspended, can be a meaningful point in a behavioral sequence. Correlate it with the process creation flags and subsequent activity.
apis.source_notes: Return-value semantics and the CREATE_SUSPENDED relationship checked against Microsoft Learn.

apis.name: ExitThread
apis.summary: Ends the calling thread and records its exit code.
apis.description: ExitThread terminates the calling thread and records the supplied exit code for the thread object. The function does not return to its caller. Other threads in the process continue to run, and the process ends when its last thread exits. The exit code can be retrieved with GetExitCodeThread while a handle to the thread remains open.

parameters.name: dwExitCode
parameters.description: The exit code to record for the thread. It can be read later with GetExitCodeThread.

apis.remarks: In C++, prefer returning from the thread function so that destructors and stack unwinding run. ExitThread terminates the thread before C++ destructors associated with the thread can execute, which is why Microsoft does not recommend it in C++ code. The thread object remains valid while handles to it are open.
apis.maldev_notes: Explicit thread termination is ordinary behavior. In analysis it matters mainly for understanding control flow and cleanup, not as an indicator by itself.
apis.defensive_notes: Thread exit events and exit codes can help correlate thread lifetime with other telemetry, but they rarely establish intent on their own.
apis.source_notes: Non-returning behavior and C++ guidance checked against Microsoft Learn (processthreadsapi.h).

apis.name: AttachThreadInput
apis.summary: Attaches or detaches the input processing mechanism of one thread to that of another thread.
apis.description: Attaches or detaches the input processing mechanism of one thread to that of another thread.
apis.prototype: BOOL AttachThreadInput(DWORD idAttach, DWORD idAttachTo, BOOL fAttach);

parameters.name: idAttach
parameters.description: The identifier of the thread to be attached to another thread. The thread to be attached cannot be a system thread.

parameters.name: idAttachTo
parameters.description: The identifier of the thread to which idAttach will be attached. This thread cannot be a system thread. A thread cannot attach to itself. Therefore, idAttachTo cannot equal idAttach.

parameters.name: fAttach
parameters.description: If this parameter is TRUE, the two threads are attached. If the parameter is FALSE, the threads are detached.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero. Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: There is no extended error information; do not call GetLastError. This behavior changed as of Windows Vista.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: By using the AttachThreadInput function, a thread can share its input states (such as keyboard states and the current focus window) with another thread. Keyboard and mouse events received by both threads are processed in the order they were received until the threads are detached by calling AttachThreadInput a second time and specifying FALSE for the fAttach parameter. The AttachThreadInput function fails if either of the specified threads does not have a message queue. The system creates a thread's message queue when the thread makes its first call to one of the USER or GDI functions. The AttachThreadInput function also fails if a journal record hook is installed. Journal record hooks attach all input queues together. Note that key state, which can be ascertained by calls to the GetKeyState or GetKeyboardState function, is reset after a call to AttachThreadInput. You cannot attach a thread to a thread in another desktop.
apis.maldev_notes: Thread APIs are common in runtimes, thread pools, debuggers, and component software. Analysts note the owning process, start address, suspend/resume state, and context changes.
apis.defensive_notes: Thread events can be correlated with process creation, image loads, and memory changes. A thread start address outside known image ranges is a useful triage signal.

example.notes: The example starts a short-lived worker thread, attaches the main thread's input queue to it with AttachThreadInput, and immediately detaches again. NtExplorer only displays the snippet; it is not executed.

apis.name: SetThreadPriority
apis.summary: Sets the priority value for the specified thread.
apis.description: Sets the priority value for the specified thread. This value, together with the priority class of the thread's process, determines the thread's base priority level.

parameters.name: hThread
parameters.description: A handle to the thread whose priority value is to be set. The handle must have the THREAD_SET_INFORMATION or THREAD_SET_LIMITED_INFORMATION access right. For more information, see Thread Security and Access Rights.Windows Server 2003: The handle must have the THREAD_SET_INFORMATION access right.

parameters.name: nPriority
parameters.description: The priority value for the thread. This parameter can be one of the following values. Priority Meaning THREAD_MODE_BACKGROUND_BEGIN 0x00010000 Begin background processing mode. The system lowers the resource scheduling priorities of the thread so that it can perform background work without significantly affecting activity in the foreground. This value can be specified only if hThread is a handle to the current thread. The function fails if the thread is already in background processing mode. Windows Server 2003: This value is not supported. THREAD_MODE_BACKGROUND_END 0x00020000 End background processing mode. The system restores the resource scheduling priorities of the thread as they were before the thread entered background processing mode. This value can be specified only if hThread is a handle to the current thread. The function fails if the thread is not in background processing mod

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero. Windows Phone 8.1: Windows Phone Store apps may call this function but it has no effect. The function will return a nonzero value indicating success.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: Every thread has a base priority level determined by the thread's priority value and the priority class of its process. The system uses the base priority level of all executable threads to determine which thread gets the next slice of CPU time. Threads are scheduled in a round-robin fashion at each priority level, and only when there are no executable threads at a higher level does scheduling of threads at a lower level take place. The SetThreadPriority function enables setting the base priority level of a thread relative to the priority class of its process. For example, specifying THREAD_PRIORITY_HIGHEST in a call to SetThreadPriority for a thread of an IDLE_PRIORITY_CLASS process sets the thread's base priority level to 6. For a table that shows the base priority levels for each combination of priority class and thread priority value, see Scheduling Priorities. For IDLE_PRIORITY_CLASS, BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS, NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS, ABOVE_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS, and HIGH_PRIORITY_CLASS processes, the system dynamically boosts a thread's base priority level when events occur that are important to the thread. REALTIME_PRIORITY_CLASS processes do not receive dynamic boosts. All threads initially start at THREAD_PRIORITY_NORMAL. apis.name: TerminateThread

parameters.name: hThread
parameters.description: A handle to the thread to be terminated. The handle must have the THREAD_TERMINATE access right. For more information, see Thread Security and Access Rights.

parameters.name: dwExitCode
parameters.description: The exit code for the thread. Use the GetExitCodeThread function to retrieve a thread's exit value.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: TerminateThread is used to cause a thread to exit. When this occurs, the target thread has no chance to execute any user-mode code. DLLs attached to the thread are not notified that the thread is terminating. The system frees the thread's initial stack. Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: The target thread's initial stack is not freed, causing a resource leak. TerminateThread is a dangerous function that should only be used in the most extreme cases. You should call TerminateThread only if you know exactly what the target thread is doing, and you control all of the code that the target thread could possibly be running at the time of the termination. For example, TerminateThread can result in the following problems: If the target thread owns a critical section, the critical section will not be released. If the target thread is allocating memory from the heap, the heap lock will not be released. If the target thread is executing certain kernel32 calls when it is terminated, the kernel32 state for the thread's process could be inconsistent. If the target thread is manipulating the global state of a shared DLL, the state of the DLL could be destroyed, affecting other users of the DLL. A thread cannot protect itself against TerminateThread, other than by controlling access to its handles. The thread handle returned by the CreateThread and CreateProcess functions has THREAD_TERMINATE

apis.name: Wow64SetThreadContext
apis.description: Sets the context of the specified WOW64 thread.
apis.prototype: BOOL Wow64SetThreadContext(HANDLE hThread, CONST WOW64_CONTEXT* lpContext);

parameters.name: hThread
parameters.description: A handle to the thread whose context is to be set.

parameters.name: lpContext
parameters.description: A WOW64_CONTEXT structure. The caller must initialize the ContextFlags member of this structure.

return.success: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
return.failure: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call GetLastError.

apis.remarks: This function allows the selective context to be set based on the value of the ContextFlags member of the context structure. The thread handle identified by the hThread parameter is typically being debugged, but the function can also operate even when it is not being debugged. This function is intended for 64-bit applications. It is not supported on 32-bit Windows; such calls fail and set the last error code to ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION. A 32-bit application can call this function on a WOW64 thread; the result is the same as calling the SetThreadContext function. Do not try to set the context for a running thread; the results are unpredictable. Use the Wow64SuspendThread function to suspend the thread before calling Wow64SetThreadContext.
apis.maldev_notes: Thread APIs are common in runtimes, thread pools, debuggers, and component software. Analysts note the owning process, start address, suspend/resume state, and context changes.
apis.defensive_notes: Thread events can be correlated with process creation, image loads, and memory changes. A thread start address outside known image ranges is a useful triage signal.

example.title: Read and restore a suspended WOW64 thread context
example.notes: The example starts a suspended 32-bit cmd.exe from SysWOW64, reads the first thread's WOW64 context, and writes the same context back with Wow64SetThreadContext before terminating the process. It requires a 64-bit Windows installation. NtExplorer only displays the snippet; it is not executed.
